cards.front: Oxidative phosphorylation is two machines: the electron-transport chain and ATP synthase. What single thing links them?
cards.back: The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. The chain pumps protons out of the matrix into the intermembrane space; ATP synthase lets them flow back and uses that flow to make ATP.
cards.quote: The two are linked by exactly one thing: the proton gradient.

cards.front: In the electron-transport chain, electrons flow spontaneously from {{c1::more negative toward more positive}} reduction potential (E°′).
cards.back: A more negative E°′ donates electrons eagerly; a more positive one grabs them hard.
cards.quote: Electrons flow spontaneously from negative toward positive, downstairs
cards.section: The energy ladder

cards.front: Rank NADH, cytochrome c, coenzyme Q and O₂ from most negative to most positive standard reduction potential (E°′), with values.
cards.back: NADH (−0.32 V) < coenzyme Q (about +0.04 V) < cytochrome c (+0.25 V) < O₂ (+0.82 V).
cards.quote: coenzyme Q just below it near +0.04 V, cytochrome c at +0.25 V, and oxygen in the basement at +0.82 V
cards.section: The energy ladder

cards.front: Using E°′(NADH) = −0.32 V, E°′(O₂) = +0.82 V and F = 96.5 kJ/(mol·V), calculate ΔE°′ and ΔG°′ for passing one electron pair from NADH to O₂.
cards.quote: NADH to oxygen: ΔE°′ = +0.82 − (−0.32) = 1.14 V, so ΔG°′ = −2 × 96.5 × 1.14 ≈ −220 kJ/mol per electron pair.
cards.section: The energy ladder

cards.front: Why do Complexes I, III and IV pump protons while Complex II does not?
cards.back: They are the three steep drops in E°′ (I: 0.36 V, about 70 kJ/mol; III: 0.21 V, about 40; IV: 0.57 V, about 110). Complex II's drop is 0.01 V, under 3 kJ/mol.
cards.why: The three steep drops together make up the whole 220 kJ/mol fall from NADH to O₂.
cards.quote: The three steep drops make up the whole fall (70 + 40 + 110 = 220), and their energy pumps protons uphill, out of the matrix.
cards.section: The energy ladder

cards.front: Pushing one proton out of the mitochondrial matrix against a typical gradient (about 0.18 V) costs about 17 kJ/mol. Complex II (succinate → Q) drops E°′ by only 0.01 V. Could Complex II pump protons?
cards.back: No. Its step releases under 3 kJ/mol, which cannot pay for even one proton, and Complex II has no proton-pumping machinery anyway. It pumps zero protons.
cards.why: This is the structural reason FADH₂ yields less ATP than NADH.
cards.quote: Under 3 kJ/mol cannot pay for one proton, and Complex II has no proton-pumping machinery anyway: it pumps zero protons, the structural reason FADH₂ yields less ATP than NADH.
cards.section: The energy ladder

cards.front: Why must the inner mitochondrial membrane be impermeable to ions?
cards.back: Because the energy of electron transport is stored as a proton gradient across it, and a gradient is only useful if it cannot leak away.
cards.quote: That is the whole foundation: a gradient is only useful if it cannot leak away.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: Coenzyme Q is a lipid-soluble carrier within the inner membrane, while {{c1::cytochrome c}} is a water-soluble carrier on the intermembrane-space face that carries one electron at a time.
cards.quote: and water-soluble cytochrome c, on the inner membrane's intermembrane-space face, carrying one electron at a time.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: Trace the electron path through Complex I (NADH-Q oxidoreductase), and give its proton count per NADH.
cards.back: NADH → FMN (a flavin) → a relay of Fe-S clusters → coenzyme Q. About 4 protons moved out per NADH.
cards.quote: NADH hands two electrons to FMN (a flavin, like FAD), which passes them through a relay of Fe-S clusters
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: What reaction does Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) catalyze, and where do its electrons go?
cards.back: It oxidizes succinate to fumarate (it is also a citric acid cycle enzyme) and passes the electrons through its FAD and Fe-S clusters to coenzyme Q.
cards.quote: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), also a citric acid cycle enzyme, oxidizes succinate to fumarate and passes the electrons through its FAD and Fe-S clusters to Q.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: Why does Complex III (cytochrome bc1) need the Q cycle?
cards.back: QH₂ carries two electrons but cytochrome c accepts only one, so the Q cycle splits each pair. Net per pair: one QH₂ in, two cytochrome c reduced, four protons out.
cards.quote: QH₂ carries two electrons but cytochrome c takes one, so the complex splits each pair by the Q cycle.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: What is the hazard built into the Q cycle at Complex III?
cards.back: It forms a short-lived Q radical (semiquinone, a Q holding one unpaired electron) that makes superoxide if it meets O₂.
cards.quote: The cost is a short-lived Q radical (a Q holding a single unpaired electron) that makes superoxide, O₂ with one extra electron, if it meets O₂
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: How does Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) avoid releasing reactive oxygen species while reducing O₂?
cards.back: Its binuclear center (a heme iron and a copper side by side) holds O₂ and every partly reduced form of it until all of it is water, so partly reduced oxygen almost never escapes.
cards.quote: It holds oxygen and every partly reduced form of it until all of it is water, so partly reduced oxygen almost never escapes.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: At Complex IV, four electrons plus four protons plus O₂ give {{c1::two waters}}.
cards.back: Cyanide and CO jam this site.
cards.quote: Four electrons plus four protons plus O₂ give two waters.
cards.section: The chain, in order

cards.front: How many protons are pumped out per electron pair by Complexes I, II, III and IV, and what are the totals for NADH and FADH₂?
cards.back: I: 4, II: 0, III: 4, IV: 2. NADH: 4 + 4 + 2 = 10. FADH₂, joining at Q: 4 + 2 = 6.
cards.quote: The column gives the rule's totals: 10 from NADH, 6 from FADH₂, whose pair joins at Q and never passes the first pump.
cards.section: The proton ledger

cards.front: Complex IV pumps 2 protons per electron pair and uses 2 more matrix protons per pair to make water. How many protons does it pump and use per whole O₂?
cards.back: One O₂ (two oxygen atoms) accepts two electron pairs. Pumped: 2 × 2 = 4. Used: 2 × 2 = 4. Total 8 per O₂, which is why per-O₂ counts look larger than the per-pair ledger.
cards.quote: Complex IV pumps 2 protons out per pair and uses 2 more from the matrix to make water.
cards.section: The proton ledger

cards.front: Complex III's own energy drop (about 40 kJ/mol) pays to move only about 2 protons. How can it release 4 protons per pair?
cards.back: Two of the four came from the matrix earlier: when Complex I or II loaded electrons onto Q, Q picked up two matrix protons, and QH₂ carried them across the membrane.
cards.quote: when Complex I or II loaded electrons onto Q, Q picked up two matrix protons with them, and QH₂ carried them across
cards.section: The proton ledger

cards.front: NADH and FADH₂ each deliver two electrons. Why does FADH₂ yield less ATP?
cards.back: FADH₂'s pair enters at Q through Complex II, which pumps nothing, so it skips Complex I's 4 protons: 6 protons instead of 10.
cards.quote: Those four protons are the entire difference: both carriers bring two electrons, and every proton they move is identical.
cards.section: The proton ledger

cards.front: Each ATP made in the matrix and delivered to the cytosol costs about 4 protons. Where do the 4 go?
cards.back: About 3 pass through ATP synthase itself (more exactly 2.7 in mammals); about 1 more drives the carriers that bring ADP and phosphate in and send ATP out.
cards.quote: about 1 more to move the goods: the carriers that bring ADP and phosphate in and send ATP out run on the same gradient.
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP

cards.front: NADH drives 10 protons out per electron pair and FADH₂ drives 6. At about 4 protons per ATP, how many ATP does each yield?
cards.back: NADH: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ATP. FADH₂: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 ATP.
cards.quote: So one NADH buys 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ATP and one FADH₂ 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP

cards.front: Why can the ATP yield per NADH (2.5) be a non-whole number?
cards.back: No chemical step ties one electron pair to a fixed number of ATP. The protons go into one shared gradient, and ATP synthase draws from it.
cards.quote: Neither has to be a whole number, because no chemical step ties one electron pair to a fixed number of ATP
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP

cards.front: Full oxidation of one glucose makes 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 4 ATP or GTP directly. Using 2.5 ATP/NADH and 1.5 ATP/FADH₂, with the malate-aspartate shuttle delivering cytosolic NADH as NADH, what is the total ATP yield?
cards.quote: Glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle make 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂, plus 4 ATP or GTP made directly
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP

cards.front: In skeletal muscle and brain, the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle hands the 2 cytosolic NADH from glycolysis to Q, as if they were FADH₂. Starting from 32 ATP per glucose with the malate-aspartate shuttle, what is the yield now?
cards.back: Each of the 2 cytosolic NADH is worth 1.5 instead of 2.5 ATP, losing 1 ATP each: 32 − 2 × 1 = 30 ATP.
cards.quote: as if they were FADH₂, worth 1.5 ATP each instead of 2.5, which gives 30.
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP

cards.front: What are the two components of the proton-motive force, and which side of the inner membrane is positive and more acidic?
cards.back: A voltage and a pH difference. The intermembrane side is positive and more acidic. In mitochondria the voltage does most of the work.
cards.quote: The proton-motive force has two parts: a voltage, with the intermembrane side positive, and a pH difference, with that side more acidic.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: Why does the electron-transport chain burn less oxygen when ADP is scarce?
cards.back: With little ADP, ATP synthase slows, so protons stop returning and the gradient builds. Each proton then costs more to push out, until electron flow nearly stalls.
cards.why: Electrons can push protons out only as fast as ATP synthase, or a leak, lets them back in.
cards.quote: With little ADP to make into ATP, the synthase slows and the chain burns less oxygen.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: Oligomycin, an ATP synthase blocker, is added to respiring mitochondria. What happens to oxygen use, and why?
cards.back: Oxygen use nearly stops, down to the leak rate. Protons cannot return through the synthase, so the gradient fills and opposes the pumps.
cards.quote: Oligomycin: protons cannot return through the synthase, the gradient fills, and oxygen use nearly stops, down to the leak rate.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: An uncoupler such as DNP (dinitrophenol), which makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons, is added to respiring mitochondria. Predict oxygen use, ATP output and heat.
cards.back: Oxygen use speeds up, ATP output falls, and heat rises. Protons rush back without passing through ATP synthase, so the gradient stays low and nothing holds the pumps back.
cards.quote: The gradient stays low, nothing holds the pumps back, and oxygen use speeds up.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: Mitochondria are treated with oligomycin until oxygen use falls to the leak rate. An uncoupler is then added. Predict oxygen use and ATP synthesis, and say what the result shows.
cards.back: Oxygen use resumes and rises; ATP synthesis stays off, because the synthase is still blocked. The chain was held back by the gradient, not by any direct link to ATP synthase.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that protons return only through ATP synthase or a leak, and electron flow can go only as fast as they return.
cards.quote: That is the rule's second half, and the return route is ATP synthase or a small leak.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: How does brown fat's uncoupling differ from that caused by the diet drug DNP?
cards.back: Brown fat uncouples on purpose, for warmth, through a regulated proton channel, UCP1. DNP made the membrane leaky with no control, and lethally.
cards.quote: Brown fat uncouples on purpose, for warmth, through a regulated proton channel, UCP1.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: Cyanide binds the binuclear center of Complex IV. Predict what happens to proton pumping, the proton gradient and ATP synthase.
cards.back: Electrons cannot reach O₂, so the chain backs up and the pumps stop. Protons keep leaking back in, the gradient runs down, and ATP synthase can no longer make ATP; it may even run backward, spending glycolytic ATP.
cards.quote: It stops the chain, so the pumps stop, while protons keep leaking back in.
cards.section: Two machines that keep each other in step

cards.front: Cyanide-poisoned mitochondria are given the uncoupler DNP. Does oxygen use recover?
cards.back: No. An uncoupler only removes the gradient's back-pressure on the pumps; with Complex IV blocked, electrons still have nowhere to fall, so the chain stays stopped.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: electron flow needs O₂ at the bottom of the ladder, and the gradient only limits the rate of a running chain.
cards.quote: Block that last step and electrons have nowhere to fall, the chain backs up

cards.front: Which complex does each inhibitor block: rotenone, antimycin A, cyanide?
cards.back: Rotenone: Complex I. Antimycin A: Complex III. Cyanide: Complex IV.
cards.quote: Rotenone blocks Complex I, antimycin A Complex III, cyanide Complex IV.
cards.section: Reading the order of the chain

cards.front: When an inhibitor blocks one complex of the electron-transport chain, which carriers become reduced and which oxidized, and why?
cards.back: Carriers upstream of the block become reduced, because electrons cannot leave. Carriers downstream become oxidized, because no electrons arrive.
cards.why: This crossover pattern, read by spectroscopy, helped work out the order of the chain before any structure was known.
cards.quote: Every carrier upstream of the block piles up reduced, because electrons cannot leave; everything downstream goes oxidized, because none arrive.
cards.section: Reading the order of the chain

cards.front: Rotenone is added to mitochondria fed an NADH-linked fuel, and the chain stops. Succinate is then supplied instead. Does the chain run, and how many protons move per pair?
cards.back: Yes. Succinate's electrons enter at Q, below the Complex I block, so the chain runs and each pair still moves 6 protons.
cards.quote: With succinate it runs, because those electrons enter at Q, below the block, and each pair still moves 6 protons.
cards.section: Reading the order of the chain

cards.front: Antimycin A is added to mitochondria. Would switching their fuel to succinate restore oxygen use, as it does after rotenone? Which carriers end up reduced?
cards.back: No. Succinate's electrons enter at Q, which is upstream of Complex III, so they still meet the block. Q stays reduced; cytochrome c and Complex IV go oxidized; oxygen use stops.
cards.why: Rests on the crossover rule plus the entry point of succinate's electrons at Q.
cards.quote: Inhibitors freeze the chain at one point, and the freeze is diagnostic.
cards.section: Reading the order of the chain

cards.front: Which sites in the electron-transport chain are among the main sources of superoxide?
cards.back: Complex I and the Complex III Qo site. Which sites dominate depends on the fuels present, and the leak is lower when mitochondria are busy making ATP.
cards.quote: Complex I and the Complex III Qo site are among the main sources, and which sites dominate depends on the fuels present.
cards.section: The price of running on oxygen

cards.front: How does Friedreich's ataxia impair the electron-transport chain?
cards.back: A GAA-repeat expansion lowers frataxin, a protein that helps build Fe-S clusters. Cluster assembly is impaired, so Fe-S enzymes of the chain and citric acid cycle lose activity.
cards.why: Sensory neurons and the heart are hit hardest.
cards.quote: a GAA-repeat expansion lowers levels of frataxin, a protein that helps build Fe-S clusters
cards.section: The price of running on oxygen

cards.front: Why does reperfusion after ischemia produce a burst of superoxide?
cards.back: Succinate builds up during ischemia. When O₂ returns, Complex II oxidizes it fast and over-reduces the Q pool; with the gradient high, electrons are pushed backward through Complex I toward NADH, making superoxide.
cards.quote: electrons are pushed backward through it, from QH₂ toward NADH, making a burst of superoxide.
cards.section: The price of running on oxygen

cards.front: On standard values, Complex I releases about 70 kJ/mol per pair and pumps 4 protons at about 17 kJ/mol each. Use this to explain why Complex I can be pushed into reverse at reperfusion.
cards.back: 4 × 17 = 68 kJ/mol against about 70 released: a margin of only about 2 kJ/mol. Running near balance, it is easily tipped backward by a high gradient and a crammed Q pool.
cards.why: Rests on the energy ladder plus the rule that the gradient's cost per proton rises as it builds.
cards.quote: Complex I's drop only just covers its four protons on standard values (about 70 kJ against 4 × 17)
cards.section: The price of running on oxygen

cards.front: A drug briefly inhibits Complex II at the moment blood flow returns to an ischemic heart. Predict its effect on the reperfusion superoxide burst.
cards.back: The burst should shrink. Blocking Complex II slows oxidation of the accumulated succinate, so the Q pool is not over-reduced and fewer electrons are pushed backward through Complex I.
cards.why: Reasoned from the lesson's mechanism: succinate oxidation by Complex II over-reduces Q, which drives reverse flow through Complex I.
cards.quote: When blood returns, Complex II oxidizes it fast and over-reduces the Q pool.
cards.section: The price of running on oxygen

cards.front: An NADH pair releases about 220 kJ/mol and a succinate pair about 150 kJ/mol. At about 17.4 kJ/mol per proton, how much energy is stored as the gradient in each case, and what fraction is that?
cards.back: NADH: 10 × 17.4 ≈ 174 kJ/mol, about 79% of 220. Succinate: 6 × 17.4 ≈ 104 kJ/mol, about 70% of 150.
cards.quote: 10 protons at about 17 kJ is about 174 of the 220 kJ an NADH pair releases
cards.section: Protons released versus charges moved

cards.front: The mammalian ATP synthase rotor has 8 c-subunits and makes 3 ATP per turn; transport adds about 1 proton per ATP. Calculate the theoretical ATP per NADH (10 H⁺) and per FADH₂ (6 H⁺).
cards.why: Proton leak and slip bring measured values down to about 2.5 and 1.5.
cards.quote: The mammalian ATP synthase rotor has 8 c-subunits and makes 3 ATP per turn, about 2.7 protons per ATP.
cards.section: Why 2.5 and not 2.7

cards.front: How does the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane compare with the inner membrane's?
cards.back: The outer membrane is porous: its VDAC channels let most small molecules and ions, up to roughly 5000 Da, through. The inner membrane is impermeable to ions.
cards.quote: Its VDAC channels let most small molecules and ions, up to roughly 5000 Da, through.
cards.section: The porous outer membrane

cards.front: How is mitochondrial superoxide cleaned up?
cards.back: Superoxide dismutase converts two superoxides to H₂O₂ and O₂; peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases (and catalase, mostly in peroxisomes) then remove the H₂O₂.
cards.quote: Superoxide dismutase converts two superoxides to H₂O₂ and O₂, then peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases
cards.section: Reactive oxygen species: numbers and cleanup

cards.front: In a hypoxic coastal dead zone, how is a fish's electron-transport chain like one poisoned with cyanide, and how does it differ?
cards.back: Alike: with no O₂ as terminal acceptor, electrons cannot leave, the chain backs up and pumping stops. Different: Complex IV itself is unblocked, so restoring O₂ restores electron flow.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the chain needs O₂ at the bottom of the ladder; cyanide removes the site, hypoxia removes the acceptor.
cards.quote: Every aerobic animal needs O₂ waiting at the bottom of the ladder; without it the chain backs up just as it does under cyanide.
cards.section: Low oxygen at ecosystem scale

cards.front: Skeletal muscle mitochondria are treated with rotenone. Can electrons from cytosolic NADH made in glycolysis still reach O₂ through the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle?
cards.back: Yes. That shuttle hands the electrons straight to Q from the intermembrane-space side, below the Complex I block, so they still pass Complexes III and IV (6 protons per pair).
cards.why: Rests on the crossover rule plus the shuttle's entry point at Q.
cards.quote: The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle (skeletal muscle, brain) hands them straight to Q from the intermembrane-space side
cards.section: The exchange rate: about 4 protons per ATP
